the repetition of information influences judgments of learning for both massed and spaced items.

repetition and feedback influence the relationship between judgments of learning ( JOLs ) and memory performance, and JOLs are often not sensitive enough to the benefits of spaced learning, even with instruction.

understanding how people use their judgments of learning and the factors that influence their judgments.
how people learn from experience and how they can use this knowledge to improve memory performance.
how metacognition is affected by practice, feedback, repetition, and instruction, and how this may affect learning and performance.

the spacing effect is a robust phenomenon in memory and learning, and people are aware of the effect, but often fail to use it when making judgments of learning, possibly due the reliance on repetition and fluency as a cue for learning.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the benefits of spaced learning may not be apparent to learners, but can be learned with experience and instruction. (PsycINFO Database Record (c) 2019 APA, all rights reserved)
the spacing effect is a robust phenomenon, and that people are aware of it when it is explicitly taught, but they often do not use it in their own learning.
the spacing effect in JOLs is influenced by the amount of repetition, feedback, and task instructions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
people often underestimate the value of spaced study, but this can be overcome by instruction and experience with spacing.
the spacing effect may be difficult to detect with JOLs, especially if the spacing effect is not emphasized in instruction.
